data.name: One Hundred Ways
data.detailed_description:
100 tricky levels to solve “One Hundred Ways” to achieve it!

The goal - make the ball reach its goal. Sounds simple - but it's not! To solve the levels, there are you will need to use some of the tools available to you. Sometimes you are going to need to think outside the box to overcome that really tricky obstacle. In December 2015 the game got a 15 level upgrade for more fun!

Features


  • 100 levels for maximum fun & challenging gaming
  • Plus 15 level for more fun, released in December 2015
  • 10 tutorial levels
  • Modern interface
  • Over 30 tools that make it either more difficult or easier for the ball to reach its goal
  • Great difficult progression
  • Real time 3D-Isometric view
  • Steam Trading Cards

reviews.review:
One Hundred Ways is an entertaining yet occasionally frustrating puzzle game that challenges players to think creatively, experiment with different mechanisms, and carefully guide a ball toward its destination. Developed and published by Sunlight Games, this independent title builds its identity around a straightforward concept that becomes increasingly complicated as new obstacles and interactive elements are introduced. Instead of depending on storytelling, combat, or exploration, it concentrates entirely on logical thinking and environmental problem-solving. Its greatest attraction is the satisfaction of discovering a solution after carefully examining a seemingly impossible arrangement, although its relatively modest presentation and occasionally awkward puzzle design prevent it from reaching its full potential.

The central gameplay mechanic involves directing a ball through various obstacles until it successfully reaches a designated endpoint. While the objective sounds simple, the challenge comes from understanding how different environmental components influence the ball's movement. Players must analyze the available pathways, recognize potential hazards, and determine which mechanisms will produce the desired result. Some situations can be resolved through straightforward observation, while others require considerable experimentation before the correct sequence becomes apparent. This balance between accessibility and complexity gives the game a recognizable personality, particularly for players who appreciate puzzles that reward patience rather than quick reflexes.

Content variety is one of the game's strongest qualities. Featuring 115 main levels alongside 10 introductory tutorial stages, it offers a substantial collection of challenges built around its core mechanics. The tutorials establish the fundamentals before gradually allowing more complicated arrangements to emerge. As players advance, familiar solutions become less reliable, encouraging them to reconsider their strategies and approach obstacles from different perspectives. The inclusion of more than 30 interactive tools and mechanisms further expands the possibilities, creating opportunities for creative solutions and unexpected combinations. However, the difficulty progression is not always equally satisfying. Certain puzzles can feel unnecessarily complicated, especially when the intended interactions are not immediately obvious.

The three-dimensional isometric presentation gives the environments a clean and recognizable appearance. Its colorful objects and relatively uncomplicated backgrounds make the game visually approachable without overwhelming players with unnecessary details. The graphics are functional rather than spectacular, placing greater emphasis on puzzle readability than artistic ambition. Unfortunately, this approach has limitations. The angled perspective can occasionally make positioning difficult to judge, particularly when several objects occupy nearby spaces. Because accurate spatial understanding is essential to solving the puzzles, these visual uncertainties can introduce frustration that feels separate from the intended intellectual challenge. The presentation accomplishes its basic purpose but lacks the refinement found in stronger puzzle games.

Another important aspect is the game's emphasis on experimentation. Rather than offering constant instructions or obvious solutions, it encourages players to investigate how individual components interact. Successfully combining different mechanisms can create rewarding moments of discovery, particularly when an initially confusing stage finally makes sense. Nevertheless, experimentation sometimes becomes repetitive when the player understands the general objective but struggles to identify the precise arrangement required. The distinction between a genuinely clever challenge and an unnecessarily obscure puzzle is important, and this game occasionally crosses that boundary. Players who enjoy methodical problem-solving will likely appreciate its approach more than those who prefer immediate feedback and consistently intuitive mechanics.

The overall pacing makes the experience suitable for both brief sessions and longer periods of concentrated puzzle-solving. Completing a few levels can provide a satisfying mental exercise without demanding a substantial time commitment. However, the absence of a narrative, meaningful character development, or substantial alternative activities means that enjoyment depends almost entirely on the strength of the puzzles themselves. Replay value is similarly limited because previously completed stages lose much of their mystery once their solutions are understood. Although alternative approaches may offer some additional entertainment, the primary motivation remains progressing through unfamiliar challenges rather than revisiting completed content.

Technically, the game is relatively lightweight and does not require particularly powerful computer hardware. Its modest visual requirements make it approachable for older systems, while its straightforward structure avoids the complexity associated with larger productions. Regarding Steam Deck compatibility, its official status remains Unknown or Unverified, as a confirmed Valve compatibility classification is not established. Although the game's modest requirements suggest that running it on portable hardware may be possible, comfortable operation cannot be guaranteed. Precise interactions and the isometric interface may require customized controls or additional adjustments, so prospective Steam Deck players should not assume a completely seamless handheld experience.

The game's reception reflects its uneven execution, with a Mixed classification on Steam suggesting that its appeal depends heavily on individual expectations. Its considerable number of puzzles and variety of mechanisms provide worthwhile entertainment, but its repetitive objective, occasionally confusing interactions, and limited visual sophistication make it difficult to recommend universally. It is best appreciated as a modest puzzle experience that prioritizes mental challenges over presentation or innovation. Players who enjoy working through mechanical problems at their own pace may discover considerable satisfaction, while those expecting polished controls, elaborate environments, or consistently inventive puzzles could find themselves disappointed.

Overall, One Hundred Ways delivers a reasonably enjoyable collection of logic-based challenges supported by a simple concept and a respectable amount of content. Its strongest moments come when careful planning and experimentation produce a satisfying solution, while its weakest emerge when unclear spatial relationships or repetitive mechanics interfere with that satisfaction. Despite its imperfections, it remains a worthwhile option for dedicated puzzle enthusiasts, particularly when available at a discount. 

Rating: 6/10
